name: Tajuosɔ

catalog_citation: Duitsman, John, Jana Bertkau & James Laesch. 1975. A survey of Kru dialects. Studies in African Linguistics 6(1): 77-103. Open-access full-issue PDF,https://journals.flvc.org/sal/article/download/107627/102943
catalog_locator: sec. 4 'Phonological Notes', p. 92; sec. 4.4 'Tone', pp. 94-95. Saved text: PDF
catalog_quote: 4. Phonological Notes. The information contained in the following phonological sketches was gleaned for the most part, from our hastily transcribed word lists and must be considered tentative. 4.1 Word shape, syllable patterns. Our lists consist primarily of one and two syllable words. Three and four syllable words are less common and usually involve compounding or reduplication. The following syllable patterns have been noted: V, VV, CV, CVV, CCV, CCVV. [...] 4.4. Tone. In regards to tone, our transcriptions are impressionistic and bear signs of undue influences from our previous language study. Some words with mid tones which are cognate with high tone words in Krahn, for example, were initially written with high tone. [...] Phonetically, there are three level tones and, in most dialects, at least one rising and at least one falling tone. As in Krahn, there is an amazing amount of tonal interaction between syllables. Most of this interaction can be explained in terms of tones which are realized in their effects upon the tones of syllables following the syllables that they are associated with. While observing this phenomenon in Krahn, Gene Bunkowske applied the term post-associative to such tones. [...] For a thorough discussion of Klae tones (Jlepe dialect) consult Nancy Lightfoot's Tones on Kru Monosyllables [1973].
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only description treats Tajuoso together with Klao as a tone language: three level tones plus at least one rising and one falling contour in most dialects, with extensive tone sandhi ('post-associated tones'). Stress and accent are never mentioned; the notes are explicitly tentative and impressionistic and rest on hastily transcribed word lists.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the authors flag their own tone transcriptions as unreliable (mid tones initially written high under Krahn influence).
new_statements.domain_note: Word lists (mostly mono- and disyllabic citation forms; syllable types V, VV, CV, CVV, CCV, CCVV); the tone remarks cover the whole Klae-Tajuoso dialect chain, not Tajuoso separately.
new_statements.identity_note: The only description (Duitsman, Bertkau & Laesch 1975) treats 'Klae' (Klao, klao1243) and 'Tajuoso' (= Tajuasohn, taju1238; clans Boo, Sece, Kulu, Kãe, Pleo per Glottolog's coding) jointly as one dialect chain; its tone remarks are not separated by variety, and its Klao tone reference (Lightfoot 1973/74) concerns the Jlepe dialect of Klao. Marchese 1989 and Vogler 2017 treat Tajuoso/'Bush Kru' as the interior dialect of Klao.

sources.note: Klae (Klao) and Tajuoso treated jointly; sec. 4 'Phonological Notes' (pp. 92-95) declared tentative; 4.1 word shapes V, VV, CV, CVV, CCV, CCVV; 4.4 Tone (pp. 94-95): three level tones plus at least one rising and one falling tone in most dialects, 'post-associated' tones; the words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the article.

Tajuasohn article has no phonology at all (refs: Ethnologue 25, Vanderaa 1991; further reading Duitsman et al. 1975); Klao article gives segment tables only, refs Duitsman et al. 1975, Lightfoot 1974, Singler 1983.
